title: Hands-on Exercise 2: First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
text:
This exercise has three parts.
Part 1 (sections 4.3 to 4.5) is data preparation: importing the childcare centre points and the subzone polygons, getting both into the same projected CRS, and converting them into the ppp and owin objects that spatstat needs.
Part 2 (sections 4.6 to 4.10) is the analysis itself. First a Clark-Evans test to answer are childcare centres randomly distributed?, then kernel density estimation to answer where are the concentrations?
Part 3 goes beyond what the chapter asks for. The chapter’s own note about bw.ppl() versus bw.diggle() is a warning that the answer depends on a choice I make, so I wanted to measure how much it depends on it, and whether the hotspots would still show up if the points were random.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
section: Alternative 1 — Quadrat test, and how much the grid choice matters
text:
Alternative 1 — Quadrat test, and how much the grid choice matters
The Clark-Evans test uses distances between points. A quadrat test uses counts in cells and a chi-square statistic. They are independent ways of testing the same null, so agreement between them is worth having.
The catch is that the quadrat test needs a grid size, and nothing tells you what it should be.

childcareSG_um <- unmark(childcareSG_ppp)

# The chapter-style single test
qt <- quadrat.test(childcareSG_um, nx = 6, ny = 4)
qt


    Chi-squared test of CSR using quadrat counts

data:  childcareSG_um
X2 = 930.15, df = 20, p-value < 2.2e-16
alternative hypothesis: two.sided

Quadrats: 21 tiles (irregular windows)



plot(childcareSG_um, pch = ".", cols = "grey40",
     main = "Observed / expected counts per quadrat")
plot(qt, add = TRUE, cex = 0.7, col = "red")








Now the same test at four different grid resolutions:

grid_sizes <- list(c(3,2), c(6,4), c(10,7), c(16,11))

quad_sens <- map_dfr(grid_sizes, function(g) {
  q <- quadrat.test(childcareSG_um, nx = g[1], ny = g[2])
  tibble(
    grid        = paste0(g[1], " x ", g[2]),
    n_quadrats  = g[1] * g[2],
    chi_squared = round(as.numeric(q$statistic), 1),
    df          = as.numeric(q$parameter),
    p_value     = format.pval(q$p.value, digits = 3)
  )
})

ImportantWhat this shows



Every grid rejects CSR, so the conclusion is robust — that is the reassuring part, and it agrees with Clark-Evans.
The chi-square statistic is not robust at all. It changes by a large factor across the four grids, because a finer grid creates more cells, more degrees of freedom, and more opportunity for observed counts to depart from expected.
So the statistic is not comparable between studies unless the quadrat size is reported alongside it. This is the zoning half of MAUP appearing in a point pattern method. The reason to prefer Clark-Evans as the headline test is that it needs no arbitrary grid — though as noted in 4.6, it substitutes a different arbitrary choice in the shape of the window.
A practical caution: with a fine grid many quadrats hold very few points, and the chi-square approximation stops being reliable. The 16 x 11 row should be read as indicative only.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
section: Alternative 2 — How far does the hotspot move when the bandwidth changes?
text:
Alternative 2 — How far does the hotspot move when the bandwidth changes?
Section 4.7.3 shows four bandwidths and leaves the choice open. Rather than assert that the choice matters, I located the single brightest point on each surface and measured how far apart those points are.

bw_list <- c(
  "bw.diggle" = as.numeric(bw.diggle(childcareSG_ppp_km)),
  "bw.ppl"    = as.numeric(bw.ppl(childcareSG_ppp_km)),
  "bw.CvL"    = as.numeric(bw.CvL(childcareSG_ppp_km)),
  "fixed 0.6" = 0.6
)

peak_of <- function(sig) {
  d  <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km, sigma = sig,
                edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian")
  df <- as.data.frame(d)
  df[which.max(df$value), c("x", "y", "value")]
}

peaks <- map_dfr(names(bw_list), function(nm) {
  p <- peak_of(bw_list[[nm]])
  tibble(method       = nm,
         sigma_km     = round(bw_list[[nm]], 3),
         peak_x_km    = round(p$x, 2),
         peak_y_km    = round(p$y, 2),
         peak_density = round(p$value, 1))
})

ImportantWhat this shows



Two things move at once.
The peak density value changes by a large multiple. A narrow bandwidth concentrates the same points into a smaller area, so the peak is far higher. This means a density number quoted without its bandwidth is not interpretable.
The peak location moves too, by kilometres in some pairs. At small bandwidth the peak sits on whichever small knot of centres is tightest. At large bandwidth it drifts towards the centre of mass of the whole eastern or central region. Those are different planning statements.
My position: report bw.ppl() as the main result, following Baddeley et al. for a predominantly clustered pattern, and state the bandwidth in the figure caption every time. bw.CvL() at over 4 km is smoothing across most of the island and should not be used here.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
section: Alternative 3 — Does edge correction actually change anything?
text:
Alternative 3 — Does edge correction actually change anything?
Every density() call above sets edge=TRUE because the chapter does. I wanted to see the size of the effect rather than trust it.
Without correction, a kernel centred near the coast spills part of its mass outside the window and that mass is lost, so density near the boundary is underestimated.

sig_use <- as.numeric(bw.ppl(childcareSG_ppp_km))

kde_edgeT <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km, sigma = sig_use,
                     edge = TRUE,  kernel = "gaussian")
kde_edgeF <- density(childcareSG_ppp_km, sigma = sig_use,
                     edge = FALSE, kernel = "gaussian")

kde_diff <- kde_edgeT - kde_edgeF

par(mfrow = c(1, 3))
plot(kde_edgeT, main = "edge = TRUE")
plot(kde_edgeF, main = "edge = FALSE")
plot(kde_diff,  main = "Difference (T - F)")









vT <- as.data.frame(kde_edgeT)$value
vF <- as.data.frame(kde_edgeF)$value

tibble(
  measure = c("Mean density, edge = TRUE",
              "Mean density, edge = FALSE",
              "Max absolute difference",
              "Mean uplift from correction (%)"),
  value = c(round(mean(vT), 3),
            round(mean(vF), 3),
            round(max(abs(vT - vF)), 3),
            round(mean((vT - vF) / pmax(vF, 1e-9)) * 100, 1))
) %>% knitr::kable(caption = "Effect of edge correction")

ImportantWhat this shows



The difference map is close to zero across the interior and positive along the coastline, which is exactly the predicted behaviour and a good check that the correction is doing what it claims.
For Singapore this matters more than it would for a compact inland study area. The island has a long, indented coastline relative to its area, so a large fraction of the study region is “near an edge”. Coastal towns like Punggol, Pasir Ris and Jurong West would have their childcare provision understated on an uncorrected map.
The same argument applies with more force in section 4.10, where the windows are single planning areas. There, almost every point is near an edge, and the neighbouring town across the boundary is not empty at all — it simply is not in the window. Edge correction fixes the geometry but cannot fix that.

title: Hands-on Exercise 2: First-order Spatial Point Patterns Analysis Methods
section: Alternative 4 — Would random points produce a hotspot this bright?
text:
Alternative 4 — Would random points produce a hotspot this bright?
This is the Xie et al. warning made testable. A KDE surface always peaks somewhere. So: if I scatter the same number of points completely at random across Singapore and compute the same KDE, how bright is that peak?
If random peaks are as bright as the observed peak, the hotspot is an artefact of smoothing. If the observed peak is far brighter than any of them, it is real.

set.seed(1234)

n_pts  <- npoints(childcareSG_ppp_km)
win_km <- Window(childcareSG_ppp_km)
n_sim  <- 99

obs_max <- max(as.data.frame(
  density(childcareSG_ppp_km, sigma = sig_use,
          edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"))$value)

sim_max <- replicate(n_sim, {
  sim_ppp <- runifpoint(n_pts, win = win_km)
  max(as.data.frame(
    density(sim_ppp, sigma = sig_use,
            edge = TRUE, kernel = "gaussian"))$value)
})

p_mc <- (sum(sim_max >= obs_max) + 1) / (n_sim + 1)

tibble(
  measure = c("Observed peak density",
              "Mean peak density under CSR",
              "Highest peak in 99 CSR simulations",
              "Monte Carlo p-value"),
  value = c(round(obs_max, 2),
            round(mean(sim_max), 2),
            round(max(sim_max), 2),
            round(p_mc, 4))
) %>% knitr::kable(caption = "Observed hotspot against 99 random patterns")

hist(sim_max,
     breaks = 20,
     col = "grey85", border = "white",
     xlim = range(c(sim_max, obs_max)),
     main = "Peak KDE value: observed vs 99 CSR simulations",
     xlab = "Maximum density on the surface")

text(obs_max, par("usr")[4] * 0.8, " observed", col = "#D1495B", pos = 2)














ImportantWhat this shows



The random patterns do produce peaks — the grey histogram is not at zero, which is the whole point. Smoothing 1,900-odd random points across Singapore reliably produces a brightest spot somewhere, and if I had only ever seen one of those surfaces I might have described it as a hotspot.
The observed peak sits far to the right of every simulated one, giving p = 0.01, the smallest value obtainable with 99 simulations. So the hotspot in the real data is not a smoothing artefact.
Two honest caveats. First, the null is CSR over the whole island, which is a weak null — it includes reservoirs and airport land where nobody would ever build a childcare centre, so it is an easy hypothesis to beat. A more demanding test would randomise within residential land only. Second, this tests only whether the maximum is unusual, not whether any particular location is a significant hotspot; that requires local statistics, which is Lesson 10.

section: Alternative 5 — More centres, or just more children?
text:
Alternative 5 — More centres, or just more children?
Everything so far shows where childcare centres are dense. That is close to useless on its own, because it is largely a map of where people live. This is Anselin’s car theft point: there are more car thefts where there are more cars.
The planning question is not where are the centres but where is provision thin relative to the children who need it. That needs a denominator.
I reuse the Census 2020 resident population table from Hands-on Exercise 1, so this section only runs if that file is present.

pop_path <- "data/aspatial/respop_census2020_agesex.csv"
have_pop <- file.exists(pop_path)
have_pop

to_count <- function(x) {
  x <- str_replace_all(x, ",", "")
  x[x == "-"] <- "0"
  as.numeric(x)
}

popdata <- read_csv(pop_path, show_col_types = FALSE) %>%
  mutate(across(-Number, to_count))

# Children of childcare age: 0-4 is the closest band available

  filter(Number != "Total", !str_detect(Number, " - Total$")) %>%
  transmute(SUBZONE_N = toupper(str_trim(Number)),
            CHILD_0_4 = Total_0_4)

provision <- mpsz_cl %>%
  mutate(SUBZONE_N   = toupper(SUBZONE_N),
         centre_count = lengths(st_intersects(., childcare_sf))) %>%
  left_join(pop_sz, by = "SUBZONE_N") %>%
  filter(!is.na(CHILD_0_4), CHILD_0_4 > 0)

  mutate(children_per_centre = ifelse(centre_count == 0,
                                      NA_real_,

extract_kml_field <- function(html_text, field_name) {
  if (is.na(html_text) || html_text == "") return(NA_character_)
  
  page <- read_html(html_text)
  rows <- page %>% html_elements("tr")
  
  value <- rows %>%
    keep(~ html_text2(html_element(.x, "th")) == field_name) %>%
    html_element("td") %>%
    html_text2()
  
  if (length(value) == 0) NA_character_ else value
